newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire army slams government, vows to hit Rwandans.
newsitem.headline: Zaire army slams government, vows to hit Rwandans.

text.p: Zaire's army, battling Tutsi rebels in the east, said on Saturday that the government was not doing enough to help it and vowed to carry the fight into Tutsi-led Rwanda once it received proper equipment.
Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, himself part-Tutsi and a target of army and popular criticism, came under growing pressure to resign.
Earlier, the government, which accuses Rwanda of fighting with the rebels, ruled out talks while foreign troops remained on its soil and said refugees should be forced to leave.
"We regret that the government is moving too slowly and has not yet given us the necessary means," Army Chief of General Staff General Eluki Monga Aundu told a Kinshasa news conference.
Reports from the east suggest Zaire's ragged army, whose soldiers have a reputation for indiscipline and looting, is hard-pressed.
Eluki accused the United Nations and international community of failing to condemn Rwandan aggression and said the U.N. refugee agency had let its vehicles be used in attacks on Zaire.

He promised a firm response against Rwandan troops once the army had the necessary equipment. "We are going to stop them, we are going to counter attack. The bombardment of Gisenyi (Rwanda) was only the beginning... we will not stop at the border."
Eluki singled out Kengo for criticism. "We thank parliament for having forced the government to explain itself," he said.
Parliament and then demonstrators who took to the streets of Kinshasa on Friday accused Kengo of not doing enough.

In Congo's capital Brazzaville, over the Zaire River from Kinshasa, representatives of opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi accused Kengo of complicity with Rwanda. "We ask the armed forces of Zaire to arrest Kengo immediately for high treason and court martial him," they said in a statement.
Zaire is the latest victim of bitter Hutu-Tutsi rivalry which has poisoned life in Rwanda and Burundi for generations.
Over a million Hutu refugees have lived in camps in eastern Zaire since 1994 when they fled Rwanda fearing reprisals or an upsurge in civil war after the genocide of Tutsis there.
Journalists and other sources say Bukavu and Uvira, where the rebel offensive began two weeks ago, are in rebel hands.
Reports from the main refugee town of Goma say troops from Rwanda were fighting alongside Tutsi rebels there.
Eluki said street fighting continued around Goma and the airport was in government hands but closed by fighting.
Kengo said on Friday the government was playing its part. "Nobody can say that the army doesn't have the means for its operations," he told reporters in the capital.
Government spokesman Boguo Makeli and Kengo said in remarks broadcast on Saturday that Zaire would boycott peace talks until foreign forces withdrew.

Boguo said the government had decided that there should be a "forced and progressive expulsion of all the Rwandan Hutu refugees" camped on Zairean territory and told the U.N. to provide food aid and protective corridors in Rwanda or Burundi.
Several hundred marchers in the capital on Friday called for Kengo's dismissal. A mob attacked Tutsi-owned shops.
Kengo dismissed the criticism. "When a war starts people look for a scapegoat," he said.

Tshisekedi claims the job of prime minister which he previously held. He is a bitter foe of Kengo, who was appointed in 1994 by the transitional parliament set up as part of Zaire's much-delayed and sometimes bloody democratic transition.

President Mobutu Sese Seko, who seized power in 1965 and ruled unchallenged until foreign and domestic pressure forced him to embrace reforms in 1990, has been in Switzerland since August, when he had surgery for prostate cancer.
